title: Tulip Mania: When One Flower Cost More Than a House
title_options: Tulip Mania: When One Flower Cost More Than a House
Tulip Mania: The First Bubble Wasn't What You Think
Tulip Mania: How a Flower Became Worth a Fortune

scenes.say: February, sixteen thirty-seven. In a crowded hall in the Dutch town of Alkmaar, an auctioneer holds up a single tulip bulb. Not a flower. A bulb, the brown, papery thing you would find in a garden shop. It sells for five thousand two hundred guilders.

At the time, a skilled craftsman might earn around three hundred guilders in a whole year. Two days later, the buyers vanish. And the strangest part? The most famous version of this story is not even true.

stat.label: for one tulip bulb, Alkmaar, 5 February 1637

scenes.say: So how did a flower drive a whole country into a frenzy? Why did it end in just a few days? And what really happened to the people caught in the middle? Let's open the ledger.

card.title: A Flower From the Sultan's Garden

scenes.say: The tulip was not Dutch at all. It came from the Ottoman Empire, where sultans grew it in their palace gardens and it became a symbol of power and wealth.
In the fifteen fifties, a Flemish diplomat at the Ottoman court, Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, is usually credited with sending tulips west. They reached a brilliant botanist named Carolus Clusius.

In fifteen ninety-three, Clusius moved to the city of Leiden to run the university's new botanical garden, and he brought his tulips with him. The flowers survived the cold, wet Dutch weather, and people who saw them wanted them. Badly. The story goes that thieves broke into his garden and stole bulbs, and those stolen bulbs helped start the Dutch tulip trade.

But one kind of tulip was worth far more than the rest. Sometimes a plain red or purple tulip would suddenly bloom with flames and feathers of colour, like this one, the legendary Semper Augustus. The Dutch called them broken tulips.

Nobody could make it happen on purpose. Growers tried everything. A plain bulb might break into stripes, or it might not, and a broken bulb was weaker and grew fewer offsets. Only in the nineteen twenties did a British scientist, Dorothy Cayley, discover the real cause: a virus, spread by tiny insects called aphids. The most expensive flowers in Europe were, in a sense, sick.
Rare, beautiful, impossible to copy, and slow to multiply. That is the perfect recipe for something people will pay almost anything for.

The Dutch Republic in the sixteen thirties was one of the richest places on Earth. Its ships traded across the world, and merchants had money to spend on beautiful, rare things. Owning a rare tulip was like owning a fine painting.

scenes.say: But tulips only bloom in spring, and the bulbs stay in the ground most of the year. So traders started signing contracts to buy a bulb later, when it could be lifted from the soil. They were trading a promise, not a flower.

By the summer of sixteen thirty-six, this trade moved into taverns. Groups of dealers met in back rooms they called colleges, bid on contracts over drinks, and paid a small fee known as wine money. Often nobody paid anything up front, and nobody had to show that they owned a bulb at all.
The Dutch even had a name for it: windhandel, the wind trade. Because what was really changing hands was air.

And then, in the winter of sixteen thirty-six, prices went wild. Even ordinary, unbroken bulbs started selling by the pound. One popular variety called Switsers rose from about one hundred and twenty-five guilders a pound at the end of December to around one thousand five hundred guilders by early February. Twelve times higher in about five weeks.

stat.label: price rise of Switsers bulbs, Dec 1636 to Feb 1637

scenes.say: People were not buying tulips to plant them. They were buying them because they believed someone else would pay more tomorrow.

Which brings us back to Alkmaar. On the fifth of February, sixteen thirty-seven, about seventy rare bulbs were auctioned for the orphaned children of a tavern owner named Wouter Winckel, who had collected some of the finest tulips in Holland. The best of them, a bulb called the Admirael van Enkhuizen, went for five thousand two hundred guilders. A Viceroy sold for more than four thousand.

find.q: Rembrandt Syndics of the Drapers Guild

scenes.say: For comparison, one of the finest houses on the canals of Amsterdam could cost around ten thousand guilders. A single bulb was worth half a mansion.
It was the very top. Within days, in the tulip capital of Haarlem, a routine sale of bulbs went quiet. Sellers named a price, then a lower price, then lower again. Nobody bid.

Word spread from tavern to tavern. If no one would buy today, then the contracts signed yesterday at sky-high prices were worth almost nothing. Buyers who had promised to pay thousands simply refused. And because these deals were made in taverns, on credit, the sellers had very little they could do.

On the twenty-third of February, flower traders from across the country met in Amsterdam to decide what to do. In the end, courts largely refused to treat the tulip contracts as real debts, and most deals were quietly settled or cancelled. The mania was over almost as fast as it began.

Now, here is the part most videos leave out. The famous version of this story, where a whole nation was ruined, comes mostly from a book written more than two hundred years later, in eighteen forty-one, by a Scottish journalist named Charles Mackay.

Mackay told wonderful stories. A sailor who ate a priceless bulb thinking it was an onion. A Viceroy bulb traded for a mountain of goods: oxen, pigs, sheep, wheat, wine, butter, a thousand pounds of cheese, a bed and a silver cup. Many of these tales came from moral pamphlets written to mock the traders.

When the historian Anne Goldgar went through the Dutch archives, she found a much smaller story. Only a few dozen people paid more than three hundred guilders for a bulb, and she could not find evidence that the crash ruined a single person or damaged the Dutch economy. The losses were real, but mostly on paper, and mostly among people who could afford them.

scenes.say: So tulip mania was real. Prices really did explode and then collapse. But the legend grew bigger every time someone retold it. Which is a lesson all by itself.

card.title: What the Tulips Still Teach Us

scenes.say: Here is what the tulip traders can still teach us, almost four hundred years later. This is not financial advice, just the pattern history keeps repeating.

First: when the only reason to buy something is that someone else will pay more later, the price does not need a crash to fall. It only needs one day with no new buyer. In Haarlem, that day came in February.

find.q: Jan van Goyen view of Haarlem

scenes.say: Second: be careful with deals made on promises and borrowed money. The traders who signed contracts with nothing paid up front felt rich right up until they had to pay.

find.q: Quentin Matsys moneylender and his wife

scenes.say: And third: check the story. Every bubble and every crash gets retold with bigger numbers and scarier endings. Before you panic, or before you jump in because everyone else is, look for the real records.

Next, we will go to London in seventeen twenty, where even Isaac Newton, the man who explained gravity, lost a fortune in a bubble. If you want that story, subscribe to Ledger of Empires. And tell me in the comments: what would you have done with a tulip worth half a mansion?
